This problem can be approached using the Pigeonhole Principle, which states that if \( n \) items are put into \( m \) containers, with \( n > m \), then at least one container must contain more than one item.

First, consider the possible remainders when a positive integer is divided by 7. These remainders are 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6. If we have a set of \( n \) distinct positive integers, we can categorize each integer based on its remainder when divided by 7. There are 7 possible remainders, so we can think of these remainders as 7 "containers."

To ensure that there exist two distinct elements \( a \) and \( b \) such that \( a + b \) is divisible by 7, we need to consider the pairs of remainders that sum to 7. These pairs are (0, 0), (1, 6), (2, 5), and (3, 4). Note that the pair (0, 0) is special because it means both \( a \) and \( b \) are divisible by 7, and their sum is clearly divisible by 7. The other pairs (1, 6), (2, 5), and (3, 4) are complementary pairs that also sum to 7.

If we have 7 integers, it is possible that each integer has a different remainder when divided by 7, and no two integers will have remainders that sum to 7. However, if we have 8 integers, by the Pigeonhole Principle, at least two of these integers must have the same remainder when divided by 7. If these two integers have remainders that are part of one of the complementary pairs, their sum will be divisible by 7. If they have the same remainder (0), their sum will also be divisible by 7.

Therefore, the smallest positive integer \( n \) such that for any set of \( n \) distinct positive integers, there exist two distinct elements \( a \) and \( b \) in the set such that \( a + b \) is divisible by 7 is \( n = 8 \).
